title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, give your name and where you're from, ask how someone is, and attach the ending that means "am/is/are" from the very first sentence.
bekal: greet with *günaydın*, *iyi günler* and *iyi akşamlar*, each at the right time
give your own name with *benim adım* and ask someone else's
attach *-im/-sin/-siniz* to say "I am / you are ..."

dialogs.title: Dialogue — İstanbul'da ilk gün
dialogs.intro: Day one in Istanbul. Budi has just come out of the airport and meets Ayşe, a member of staff at the language school who has come to pick him up.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Merhaba, hoş bulduk. Benim adım Budi.
lines.id: Hello, thank you. My name is Budi.
lines.literal: hello, pleasant found-we. my name-my Budi.

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.id: Nice to meet you, Mr. Budi. How are you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm fine, thank you. How are you?

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.text: Ben de iyiyim, sağ olun. Nerelisiniz?
lines.id: I'm fine too, thanks. Where are you from?
lines.literal: I too fine-I-am, healthy be-you. where-from-you-are?

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.id: That's so far! Do you speak Turkish?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: A little. I'm a student, I'm learning Turkish.

lines.speaker: Ayşe:
lines.id: This way, the car is here.

notes: **Hoş geldiniz demands a fixed reply.** Literally "you came pleasantly", and the answer is always *hoş bulduk* — "we found (everything) pleasant". Not *teşekkür ederim*. This pair is used everywhere: in people's homes, in shops, even on planes.

**There are two words for "you", and picking the wrong one stings.** *Sen* is for friends, people your age, children. *Siz* is for people you've just met, older people, or customers — like *vous* in French. When in doubt, use *siz*: being too polite never offends; being too familiar can.

**Bey and Hanım go after the first name, not the surname.** *Budi Bey*, *Ayşe Hanım*. Roughly "Mr. Budi" and "Ms. Ayşe" — but note the order: name first, title after, like everything else in this language.

**"Am/is/are" never stands alone.** *Öğrenciyim* = student + I-am. *İyiyim* = fine + I-am. There's no separate word for "am": it is attached to the end of the last word. If that word ends in a vowel, a linking *y* slips in — *iyi-y-im*, not *iyiim*.

blocks.text: These twelve phrases are not grammar material — they're an emergency kit. Memorize them whole now, understand how they work later.

blocks.text: *Rica ederim* literally means "I request" — and yet it's the standard reply to thank you, just as odd as "don't mention it" if you think too hard. Another one that's just as common: *bir şey değil* ("it's nothing").

blocks.title: One sentence that changes your time in Turkey
items: *Türkçe öğreniyorum. Türkçe konuşabilir miyiz?* — "I'm learning Turkish. Can we speak Turkish?"

Unlike in many other countries, Turks rarely switch to English — often simply because they can't. What happens more often is the opposite: they speak too fast because they're delighted you're trying. The sentence above, plus *yavaş lütfen*, solves both.

blocks.text: Notice that three of the greetings use the plural — *günler*, *akşamlar*, *geceler*, literally "good days", "good evenings". Turkish feels a wish is warmer in the plural; you'll meet this pattern again in *teşekkürler* and *kolay gelsin*.

blocks.title: Don't mix them up
items: *Güle güle* must NOT be said by the person leaving. Literally "laughing, laughing" — a wish for someone else's journey. The one leaving says *hoşça kal* (to one person) or *hoşça kalın* (to several people or to someone you address formally).
If you're unsure which is which, *görüşürüz* is safe for anyone, going either way.

sections.title: Ben kimim? — the ending that means "am/is/are"

blocks.text: Turkish has no word for "am/is/are". Instead there are **person endings** attached to a noun or adjective. Since the ending already says who the subject is, the pronoun in front can be dropped — and it usually is.

The third person singular has no ending at all in conversation: *O öğretmen* — "he/she (is a) teacher". The ending *-dir* exists, but it sounds formal: it shows up on notices, packaging and in the news (*Kapı kapalıdır* — "the door is closed").
To say "not", add the separate word *değil* — and the person ending moves onto it: *Öğretmen değilim* (I'm not a teacher), *Türk değilsin* (you're not Turkish), *Hazır değiliz* (we're not ready).

The ending *-li/-lı/-lu/-lü* means "person from" or "having". Attach it to a place name: *İstanbullu* (someone from Istanbul), *Ankaralı*, *Jakartalı*, *Endonezyalı*. Then add the person ending after it: **Endonezyalıyım** — I'm from Indonesia.

blocks.title: Why "iyiyim" has a y in it
items: Turkish doesn't like two vowels colliding. If a word ends in a vowel and the ending also starts with one, a linking consonant is inserted — here **y**: *iyi + im* → *iyiyim*, *Ayşe + im* → *Ayşe'yim*.
These linking letters will keep appearing throughout the course, in three different forms: *y*, *n* and *s*. Each time, the reason is the same: to keep two vowels from bumping into each other.
